claims.text: The starting AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA has a uniform, fine lamellar structure.
The starting alloy provides good strength and plasticity.
The starting alloy has inadequate long-term thermal stability, creep resistance, and corrosion resistance for industrial use.
Co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 with trace Y and Hf will improve performance under temperature fluctuations, long-term loading, creep, and corrosion.
Y and Hf preferentially segregate to grain boundaries and surfaces in the alloy.
Y and Hf segregation promotes formation of a continuous, adherent, and thermally stable oxide layer.
Y and Hf segregation enhances grain-boundary cohesion.
The Y/Hf-promoted oxides inhibit grain-boundary sliding and thereby reduce creep.
Y and Hf co-doping suppresses grain coarsening during exposure at 900 °C.
The Y/Hf-associated oxide layer acts as a barrier against corrosive attack.
Y and Hf co-doping maintains the alloy's fine lamellar structure during high-temperature exposure.
Maintaining the fine lamellar structure enables retention of high strength and ductility.
The YHf-doped alloy will have a lower creep rate than the undoped alloy.
The YHf-doped alloy will retain strength and ductility better at elevated temperature than the undoped alloy.
The YHf-doped alloy will exhibit less oxide-scale spallation than the undoped alloy.
Exposure near 900 °C is an appropriate regime for evaluating the proposed thermal-stability and hot-corrosion effects.
Molten-salt media can be used to test hot corrosion of the base and YHf-doped alloy.
The proposed improvement is expected to apply to single-phase alloys.
The intervention is applicable to both casting and laser-cladding processing routes.
The optimal Y and Hf concentrations, segregation behavior under coupled loading, and long-term service stability remain undetermined.

contradictions.description: The target is described as a fine lamellar eutectic alloy whose lamellar structure should be maintained, but the boundary states that the improvement applies to single-phase alloys. A eutectic lamellar structure is intrinsically multiphase, and the cited record identifies FCC and BCC/B2 phases.
